awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Development of A Novel Visible-Light Phase Shifter and Intraocular Lens to Improve Vision for Those With Age-Related Macular Degeneration
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is a novel implantable lens for shifting the phase of visible-light phase to mitigate vision loss due to age related macular degeneration and damaged retinal regions. Age-related macular degeneration is a chronic and progressive eye disease affecting more than 20 million people in the US and 200 million people worldwide and often results in irreversible blindness. No permanent solution currently exists for treating age-related macular degeneration and mitigating vision loss until surgical interventions may be required. This proposed system aims to provide a permanent means for shifting the area of focus of visible light onto a viable region of the retina for restoring vision to help patients complete common everyday activities, reduce costs of care associated with vision loss and reduce the resulting emotional or health-related burden of macular degeneration. 

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to complete the development of an electronic implantable intraocular lens through a novel implantable low power rechargeable visible-light phase shifter and subsequent optical phased arrays. Current optical phased arrays require high-power consumption with a large footprint, impeding their effectiveness in a commercializable, fully implantable biocompatible device. This project aims to address several critical technical hurdles by developing an energy-efficient metal-oxide-semiconductor capacitor, small-form factor optical phased array in an intraocular implantable device capable of electronically adjusting and shifting visible light frequencies to alternative viable regions of the retina. The study team will conduct systematic modeling to map the performance of key functions and determine the optimal waveguide geometry. Once finalized, the study team will fabricate the devices and measure their performance using standard optical benchmarking measurements relative to a reference waveguide.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report — NSF SBIR Phase I Award 2451179

 

Glaive Medical Optics, Inc. (GMO) used this NSF Small Business Innovation Research Phase I award to establish the technical feasibility of its Targeted Digital Vision (TDV) device, a new digital class of eye lens replacement prosthetics intended to restore functional vision for people losing their central sight to age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

AMD affects more than 18 million Americans, and roughly 1.5 million have an advanced form of the disease. It is progressive and uncurable, and damages the retina starting with the central vision. Over time, the center of the retina slowly stops working while the surrounding retina remains healthy. Patients lose the ability to read, recognize faces, and drive. Today’s options are limited: drugs can slow the disease but do not restore lost sight; retinal prostheses are designed for patients who are already blind and require complex retinal surgery; and fixed-magnification implants cannot be adjusted as the disease progresses. No device serves the long intermediate period when a patient still has usable retina but is losing everyday function.

TDV addresses this gap. The device replaces the eye’s natural lens, in the same location and through the same routine procedure used in cataract surgery, performed about four million times per year in the United States. Small cameras on the implant capture the scene, the image is processed digitally, and a miniature display projects the image onto the part of the patient’s retina that still works. Because the image is digital, a clinician can shift, magnify, or enhance it during a routine office visit as the disease changes, with no additional surgery. The implant has no battery but is rather continuously powered wirelessly by ordinary-looking eyeglasses. When the glasses are removed, the device becomes a passive lens and the patient’s remaining natural vision is preserved.

The award originally funded development of an integrated-photonics beam-steering approach to move the image on the retina. Early in the project, an engineering assessment showed that this approach would require years of custom photonic fabrication before any clinical device could be built. With NSF approval, the project objectives were revised in January 2026 to achieve the same key clinical function, a steerable image on surviving retina, using digital image remapping on a micro-LED display built from components that already exist at manufacturing scale. This substantially shortened the path to patients.

Under the revised objectives, the Phase I team built and tested oversized benchtop demonstrators for each of the three highest-risk parts of the system. First, the complete optical chain was built and tested. The team demonstrated live-scene capture and projection with the target components. Separately, the team also showed that two independently generated images, representing both a wide, lower-resolution peripheral view and a narrow, high-resolution central view, can merge in the optics into a single image on a model retina, with each image independently steerable. Second, the team developed the wireless power system and demonstrated that sufficient power can be delivered using the near-field communication (NFC) protocol, with built-in power regulation to manage delivered power based on feedback from the implant. Furthermore, the prototype electronics power requirements were measured to be well under the total available delivered power and also well below the level that would harm the eye. Third, the team designed a three-layer materials approach for protecting the electronics inside the eye for more than a decade, including a rigid electronics-and-optics core, a thin conformal moisture barrier, and a soft biocompatible outer body shaped like a conventional lens implant, and defined the experiments needed to prove it.

Intellectual merit: The project demonstrated that a multi-channel digital projection system can deliver a single, steerable, resolution-matched image to the retina from within the eye’s lens capsule, and that this can be powered wirelessly at safe levels. It also identified where existing implant-qualification standards do not apply to cavity-free encapsulation, a gap relevant to the broader field of miniaturized active implants.

Broader impacts: If successful, TDV would offer millions of people with AMD a way to keep reading, recognizing loved ones, and living independently, through a familiar outpatient surgery available in community ophthalmology practices rather than a few specialized centers. The device is also designed to adapt as the disease progresses, and its clinical adjustments over time create a new, non-invasive record of disease progression that could support future research and treatment.

Phase I established feasibility of the concept on benchtop demonstrators. The remaining work is integration and miniaturization to intraocular scale: optimizing the wireless power link, proving the moisture-barrier process, and developing the custom chips for the commercial device. GMO is pursuing NSF Phase II funding and private investment to complete a design-frozen, manufacturable device with preclinical evidence in support of a future first-in-human study.
